Summary: The paper compares generation strategies for writing OMIM phenotype entries from exactly the papers the curators cited, holding the model (Claude Opus 5.5), sources, guards, claim-level audit and scoring fixed. 100 entries with 2-12 references (515 papers; 96 full text, 345 abstract-only, 74 title-only via open access) are drawn from five creation-era bands. Strategies form three paradigms: read-and-write (direct reading in one prompt; an agentic curator), extract-then-write (evidence graph; case table) and memory-first (recall, then verify), plus a memory-only control and three add-ons (second-hand passages, reconciled case database, learned guide). The primary endpoint, 'OMIM facts conveyed', judges each of 6,652 atomic facts, split once from OMIM's variant-centred allelic-variant paragraphs (deposited in ClinVar), as present/partly/absent/contradicted in the draft text citing that paper. Main results: hiding the full text of the same papers lowers coverage from 79.8% to 36.1% (46 entries, +43.7 points, 45/0/1; Table 23); at the main settings the agent and evidence graph are not distinguishable from direct reading and the case table trails by 1.9 points (Table 1); in a matched ablation on 38 selected entries the evidence graph leads by 1.8 points; four 'reading better' variants on 41 held-out entries give gains of 1.6-3.3 points, with a completeness pass at +2.6 without loss of judged fidelity (Table 29, 32); a planted-error stress test shows the audit's best-verdict rule hides added citations and that deleted qualifiers (zygosity, hedges, 'one family') are mostly missed (Figure 4, Tables 49-50). All judgements are made by the writer's model family and none was validated by a person.
Strengths: Clean controlled design: the source set is fixed to the curators' reference list, one model does every role, and the guards, audit and scoring are shared (Section 3, Figure 1), so the strategy is the only manipulated variable in the main comparison. This is a useful contrast to the literature the paper cites, where designs are compared across tasks, models and scorers.

The within-paper access manipulation (Section 4.1, Table 23) is the strongest result: hiding the full text of the same 91 papers, with memory and paper identity held constant, moves coverage by +43.7 points (95% CI +38.3 to +49.1; 45 better, 0 worse, 1 tied), and the no-repair rescoring makes the comparison like for like. The second-hand-passage arm (+4.9 points) quantifies a realistic partial substitute.

Fact lists are split once, without sight of any draft, and reused for every strategy (Section 3.3), removing per-draft denominator drift; the earlier per-draft scoring is kept as a row and preserves the ordering (Table 6). Credit-anywhere checks show pooling strategies are not penalised by the per-paper crediting rule (Appendix E).

Statistical reporting is unusually careful: paired bootstrap intervals over entries with better/worse/tied counts and exact sign tests, Holm adjustment for secondary measures (Table 8), an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis (Table 11), run-to-run replicates and judge re-runs used as a noise yardstick rather than a test (Appendix E, Table 20), and an explicit primary/secondary/post hoc/exploratory status for every analysis (Tables 2-3). Corrected analyses are disclosed (Appendix M.4).

The decomposition by whether the supplied text states a fact (Figure 2b-c, Table 19, Figure 6, Table 17) explains why designs differ little: reading strategies convey 91-94% of stated facts, and only about 4% of all facts are missed although stated. The reading-better arms then recover gains where this analysis predicts, on stated full-text facts (+4.5 for the completeness pass; Figure 3b, Table 29), with prompts frozen before the held-out run.

The audit stress test (Section 4.5, Figure 4, Tables 49-52) gives concrete, actionable blind spots: added citations pass 0/30 even though the added paper's own verdict was 'unsupported' for 176/176 claims, zygosity deletions are caught 0/8, and 4-7% of (claim, cited paper) pairs in real multi-citation paragraphs are not supported. The unaltered re-audit control (0/60, 0/113 flagged) is a sensible addition.

The memory-only control by creation era and on entries created in 2026 (Figure 5, Table 16, Appendix M.2) is a practical contamination probe: memory gene F1 falls from 88.9-100% in older bands to 41.2% (620000 onward) and 30.0% (2026), while direct reading stays at 100%.
Costs, completion, safety-filter stops and deviations from design are reported in full (Tables 5, 12, 28, 33, 36-38), and per-entry drafts, verdicts and scores are released.
Weaknesses: No judgement is validated by a person, and one model family writes, extracts, splits the reference, marks facts, judges what the text 'states' and audits (Section 3.3; Limitations i-ii). The 95.7% agreement between two judgings (Appendix E) is self-consistency, not validity. Because the strategy differences of interest are 0.5-2 points, a modest systematic judge bias (e.g., self-preference for certain phrasings or for the structure an intermediate representation produces; Panickssery et al., 2024) could reorder them. Even a small stratified expert sample of fact marks, 'stated' verdicts and audit verdicts, with chance-corrected agreement, or a second judge family on a subset, is needed before the levels and orderings can be relied on.

The headline matched-settings result is presented more strongly than the appendix supports. The abstract and Section 1 report that with settings matched the evidence graph leads by 1.8 points (95% CI 0.4 to 3.3). Appendix F and Table 22 show that on the same 38 entries the main-setting evidence graph is already +1.0 (-0.9 to +2.8), and the matched change itself is only +0.8 (-0.5 to +2.1). The sign also reverses between the 19 high-full-text entries (-1.2) and the other 19 (+3.1). The 1.8-point lead therefore mostly reflects which 38 entries were averaged (a non-random subset weighted towards full text, chosen after the main comparison) rather than the matching. It is also a secondary analysis with no multiplicity adjustment. The abstract should say this, or drop the claim.

The primary endpoint is recall-only and not controlled for length. Drafts make about twice as many statements per paper as the reference has facts, and only about 24% of statements have a counterpart (Appendix H). The reading-better arms lengthen drafts by about a third (10,802 to 14,412 characters; Table 33), and the extract-then-write drafts carry 12-17% more audited claims (Table 6: 113.5 and 117.9 vs 101.0). The audit checks fidelity, not relevance, so gains of 1-3 points may partly reflect verbosity. A precision-like measure against the reference, or a length-matched analysis, is missing. Separately, variant precision counts a variant OMIM does not list as a miss even when the paper reports it (Table 10), which conflates errors with legitimate extras and penalises the extract-first designs.

The regime limits the external validity of the strategy comparison. Entries have 2-12 references that fit in one prompt for a frontier long-context model, and 2,669 of 6,239 compared facts are not stated in any supplied text (Table 19). The settings that motivate agents and extract-first designs (many relevant papers, smaller context windows) produced no comparison: 0 of 4 large entries were completed by every strategy (Appendix K.2), and the 30-75-reference tier is reported without findings (Appendix M.1). 'Access dominates strategy' is therefore established only where the strategies are least expected to differ. The access effect is itself expected, as the authors note in Section 1: the reference is variant-centred and its details live in full text.

The reference is indirect. The task is writing a phenotype entry, but scoring uses allelic-variant paragraphs from OMIM gene entries as deposited in ClinVar, and only the draft text citing that paper (Section 3.1; Limitation iv). Narrative phenotype content, which is most of each draft, is checked only by the same-model audit. The 43.7-point access effect and the strategy ordering are specific to this variant-centred slice.

The benchmark contribution is weaker than claimed in contribution (1). The fixed fact lists and curator text are not redistributed. A rebuilt reference must be split again, and how much a fresh split moves levels or differences was not measured (Section 3.1 'Reuse'; Reproducibility statement). The interface exposes no temperature or seed, and the model's safety filter decides completion. A new strategy therefore cannot be scored on the same denominators. The work is better described as a controlled study with released drafts and scores than as a reusable benchmark.

Analytic flexibility is high relative to the effect sizes. Two measurement rules changed during the study, including making completion symmetric after the first analysis had put the evidence graph 2.1 points below direct reading (Section 3.3, Appendix M.4). Several key restrictions are post hoc (stated/not stated, the no-repair rescoring, stopped-revision handling). The primary endpoint is unadjusted across five comparisons, and the main strategies were developed on the entries they are evaluated on (Limitation viii). Labelling is transparent, but with more than 50 tables and differences of 0.5-2 points, the ordering claims would benefit from a preregistered confirmatory run on fresh entries; only 20 entries created in 2026 are held out for the main strategies.

Safety-filter stops act as an uncontrolled selection mechanism. Completion differs by strategy (Table 5), and the same entries (118210, 617232, 621030) are lost by the evidence graph, the case table and the completeness arms (Tables 5, 28), which suggests the stops depend on content. The completeness pass's mean gain turns negative when lost entries count as zero (-3.5 and -4.8; Table 31). Its stated benefit therefore depends on a fallback rule adopted after review, and the reasons for stops are invisible (Limitation ii).

The released-system comparisons (Section 4.4, Appendix J) are too weak to inform the main question. PaperQA2 ran without its agent and GraphRAG on only 4 entries, STORM produced nothing, both systems answered six section questions rather than writing an entry, and a small shared embedder (bge-small, 512-token inputs) replaced the defaults. They take up main-text space while carrying no claim. Running direct reading through the same six-question protocol, as Limitation xi suggests, would at least separate the protocol from the design.

Clarity suffers from density and hedging. The abstract packs many numbers and qualifiers. The reader has to track many conditions at once: repaired vs unrepaired, mean vs pooled, the 93/46/41/38/35/20-entry sets, fixed vs per-draft scoring, and primary vs post hoc status. Key definitions ('like for like', 'completes', 'stated') are concentrated in one compressed paragraph of Section 3.3. A main-text table mapping each claim to its evidence, entry set and status would help considerably.
Questions: Can you add expert validation on a stratified sample, covering fact marks (present/partly/absent/contradicted), 'stated' judgements and audit verdicts, with chance-corrected agreement? Can you also re-judge a subset with a different model family to estimate self-preference and correlated errors between the 'stated' and 'conveyed' judgements?

For the matched ablation, will you revise the abstract and Section 1 to report that the main-setting evidence graph is already +1.0 on the same 38 entries and that the matched change is +0.8 (-0.5 to +2.1)? Was the 38/40-entry subset fixed before per-entry main-comparison results were seen?

Can you report a length-controlled view of the primary endpoint for each strategy and reading-better arm, for example coverage per 1,000 characters or the share of per-paper statements with a reference counterpart, so that gains from completeness or merging can be separated from added verbosity?

Of the variants generated by the evidence graph and case table that OMIM does not list (Table 10), how many are reported in the cited papers? That would separate extraction errors from legitimate extras.

Do the safety-filter stops cluster by paper, topic, access level or creation era? Please characterise the entries lost across arms (e.g., 118210, 617232, 621030) and say whether dropping them could favour any strategy.
How sensitive are the paired differences, not only the levels, to the half-credit for 'partly present'? Table 6 reports full-credit-only levels, but not full-credit-only differences or intervals.

Can you quantify how much a fresh split of the reference by the same procedure moves levels and paired differences, for example by re-splitting 20-30 entries? This bears directly on whether others can reuse the benchmark.

Is there any setting in which extract-first or agentic designs could be compared where they are motivated, such as a smaller-context model, or entries above the single-prompt budget with a writer that is not stopped? Without one, how far should readers generalise the 'strategy matters little' conclusion?

Given that deleted zygosity and 'one family' qualifiers were not caught (0/8, 0/2; Table 50), and that these matter clinically, did you consider a qualifier-specific check, or a rule that flags a claim when any cited paper fails it? What false-flag rate would the latter have on the multi-citation paragraphs of Table 52?
Limitations: Every judgement (fact splitting, fact marking, 'stated', audit) comes from the writer's model family, and none was validated by a person. Levels, the stated/not-stated contrast and the audit's catch rates are therefore unverified, which the paper acknowledges.
Only one writer model was used. Transfer of the access effect and the strategy ordering to other model families, especially smaller-context models, is untested.
The reference is variant-centred allelic-variant text plus HPO, gene and inheritance tables. Phenotype narratives are not compared, and most draft content has no reference counterpart.
Only open-access text without supplementary material was used. The access effect is measured against a reference that curators wrote from full papers and supplements.
The regime is small (2-12 references per entry, inputs that fit in one prompt), and no comparison exists for large reference sets because of safety-filter stops.
The main strategies were developed on their evaluation entries. Held-out evidence for them is limited to 20 entries created in 2026.
The curator-derived fact lists cannot be redistributed, and a re-split's stability is unmeasured, which limits reuse as a benchmark.

Generated drafts could be mistaken for curated content. The paper rightly requires that they be marked as machine generated. The audit's blindness to deleted zygosity, hedges and over-citation should be stated prominently for any clinical-facing use, since a passed audit does not certify correctness or completeness.
